title: The GitHub Flow: Branches & Pull Requests

options.text: A Git command that downloads changes
A GitHub feature that proposes merging one branch into another, with review and checks
A way to delete a branch

questions.explanation: A pull request is a GitHub feature to propose merging a branch, bundling the diff, automated checks, and a review conversation. (It is not the same as git pull.)

questions.prompt: In the GitHub flow, where do you do your work?

options.text: On a branch off main, then open a pull request
In a separate repository each time
Only in the GitHub web editor

questions.explanation: GitHub flow keeps main deployable: you branch off main, commit, push, and open a PR — you don't commit straight to main.

questions.prompt: Which are steps in the GitHub flow? Select all that apply.

options.text: Open a pull request to propose the merge
Commit all changes directly to main as the normal path

questions.explanation: GitHub flow is branch → commit → push → PR → review → merge → delete branch. Committing directly to main bypasses the review the flow is built around.

questions.prompt: GitLab's equivalent of a GitHub 'pull request' is called a ______ request.
questions.explanation: GitLab uses the term 'merge request' for the same concept — proposing to merge one branch into another.

questions.prompt: Why are small, focused pull requests recommended?

options.text: GitHub charges per line in large PRs
They are faster to review, safer to merge, and easier to revert
Large PRs cannot be merged at all

questions.explanation: Review effort grows with PR size. Small, single-purpose PRs get reviewed quickly, are less risky to merge, and are simpler to revert if needed.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Propose merging a branch into another
Approve or request changes on a PR

questions.explanation: A PR proposes a merge, review gates it, GitHub flow is the overall workflow, and main stays deployable.
